The Story of Kartikeya Muni

I bow to Lord Jina, whose supreme eye of omniscience sees the subtlest things in the universe, who is the embodiment of purity and the giver of all happiness, and I write the story of Kartikeya Muni.

King Agnidatt of Kartikpur and Queen Veervati had a daughter named Krittika. Once, during the eight-day festival, she observed an eight-day fast. On the final day, after worshipping the Lord, she brought back the flowers offered to the Lord and gave them to her father. Seeing her divine beauty at that moment, her father Agnidatt's mind was disturbed. Overcome by lust, the sinful king gathered many teachers of other faiths and some Jain monks and asked, "O great yogis, please tell me — can I, or can someone else, be the master of the jewel born in my house?"

As soon as the king finished his question, a single voice came from all sides: "Maharaj, you alone can be the master of that jewel, no one else." But the Jain monks, after deep thought, answered differently: "O King, it is true that you are the master of the jewel born here — but leaving aside the jewel of a daughter. Her mastery you can exercise only as a father, not in any other way."

The king did not like this wholesome answer from the Jain monks — and how could he? When do sinners ever appreciate good advice? Enraged, he banished those monks from the country and married his own daughter. Truly, those who are sinful and lustful, destined to suffer in lower births — where is dharma for them, where is shame, where is morality, where is good sense?

After some time, Krittika bore two children — a son named Kirtikeya and a daughter named Veermati. Veermati was very beautiful. She was married to King Kronch of Rohed city and lived there happily.

Meanwhile, Kirtikeya grew up. He was now about fourteen years old. One day he was playing with his companion princes. They were all wearing fine clothes and ornaments given by their maternal grandfathers. Upon asking, Kirtikeya learned that these gifts came from the mothers' fathers. He asked his own mother, "Mother, who is my maternal grandfather? Why have I never been to his house?" Krittika, unable to hide the truth any longer, told him everything — how his own father, King Agnidatt, had married her in violation of all dharma.

Hearing this, Kirtikeya was filled with shame and anger. He could not bear the disgrace. He left the palace and wandered in the forest. There he met a great Jain monk who taught him the path of dharma. The monk explained that all worldly relationships are impermanent and that true happiness lies not in the body or its pleasures but in the purity of the soul. Kirtikeya's heart was transformed. He took initiation as a monk and practised intense austerities.

Through dedicated spiritual practice, Kirtikeya destroyed his karmas and attained omniscience. He became a great teacher, guiding countless souls to the path of liberation. His mother Krittika too, hearing of his achievements, repented for her past and eventually attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the most shameful origins can be transcended through spiritual practice. Kirtikeya, born of an incestuous union, rose above his disgrace through the power of dharma and attained the highest spiritual goal. The wise should not be defined by their past but by their present actions and their aspiration for liberation.
